name: Mal
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Filbeck, David. 1976. Mal (Thin). In William A. Smalley (ed.), Phonemes and Orthography: Language Planning in Ten Minority Languages of Thailand, 239-257. Pacific Linguistics C-43. Canberra: Australian National University. Open online edition.
catalog_locator: p.251, sections SYLLABLE STRUCTURE and word STRUCTURE; p.241 fn.1; p.252 compounds and word stress vs sentence stress; pp.248-250 tones and intonation.
catalog_quote: In addition to major syllables, minor syllables also occur. These are syllables that occur only with weak stress. Minor syllables will have one vowel preceded by one, two or three consonants followed by zero or one consonant: (C)C(C) V (C). ... WORD STRUCTURE. Word structure consists of one major syllable with or without one (or sometimes two) preceding minor syllables. Because words contain only one major syllable, all words, regardless of number of syllables, are characterised by a single stress: /pathiaʔ/ [pa'thiaʔ] 'evening'; /tabapǎn/ [taba'pǎn] 'to Mr Pan'. [p.241 fn.1] A major syllable is a syllable which may carry primary stress. Minor syllables may never be so stressed. [p.252] A word that occurs with a long vowel in isolation takes a short vowel in a minor syllable of a compound word: /nthuʔuaŋ/ [nthu'ʔuagŋ] 'vegetable', from /nthuu/ [n'thu.] 'leaf' and /ʔuaŋ/ ['ʔuagŋ] 'wood'. ... Stressless minor syllables are lower pitched than stressed major syllables: /pathak/ [pà'thagk] 'forever'; /pamual/ [pà'muadl] 'stick for planting rice'.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mal words are sesquisyllabic: one major (full) syllable optionally preceded by one or two minor syllables; only the major syllable can bear stress and it is always word-final, so word stress falls on the last syllable ([pa'thia?], [taba'pan]); in compounds the first member is reduced to an unstressed short-vowel minor syllable and stress stays on the final syllable ([nthu'?uago] 'vegetable').
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress described; minor syllables have 'weak stress' and lower pitch. A separate system of three SENTENCE stresses (primary/secondary/tertiary, pp.249-250) is intonational, with the contour crest on the last word of the sentence.
new_statements.exceptions: None at word level. Emergent rising tone (mainly on Thai/Myang loans) coexists with stress; minor syllables in compounds shorten long vowels; p.252 notes word stress and sentence stress 'coalesce' and that major syllables in tertiary sentence-stress position take on minor-syllable characteristics.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement (section 'Word structure'), illustrated with citation forms and a compound; author explicitly separates word stress (traditional marks) from sentence stress (numerals), p.249 fn.1.
new_statements.identity_note: Filbeck's 1976 chapter describes the Ban Pha Nam Yoi - Ban Toei dialect of Mal (Pua and Chiang Klang Districts, Nan Province), i.e. his 'Mal dialect B' (the largest Mal dialect, ~3,000 speakers; cf. Filbeck 1978:33, 1991:232). This is Mal proper = Glottolog mall1246 [mlf], sister of Prai/Pray (phai1238) within T'in (Mal-Phrai).

tone_statements.citation: Chommanad Intajamornrak (ชมนาด อินทจามรรักษ์). 2009. เส้นทางสู่การเป็นภาษาวรรณยุกต์ของภาษามัล-ไปรที่พูดในจังหวัดน่าน [On becoming a tonal (language) of Mal-Pray spoken in Nan province]. PhD dissertation (อักษรศาสตรดุษฎีบัณฑิต, Linguistics), Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok. 392 pp. Advisor: Theraphan Luangthongkum.
tone_statements.quote: The pitch pattern of the homophonous pairs in the non-tonal varieties are the same, whereas, there are two pitches in the word pairs which can distinguish the meaning, i.e. /high/ [high falling and high level] and /low/ [low rising] in the tonal varieties. Therefore, it can be concluded that MTY and MYW are tonal language having two tones /high/ and /low/. These two tones are also assigned to Tai Yuan loanwords.

tone_statements.citation: Chommanad Intajamornrak. 2009. The Fundamental Frequencies of Tai Yuan Tones Spoken by Lua' (Mal) Speakers in Nan Province, Thailand. Manusya: Journal of Humanities 12(3): 20-33.
tone_statements.quote: Lua’ (Mal), a Mon-Khmer language, has been reconstructed as a non-tonal language. However, it has been found that the Lua’ (Mal) spoken in Ta Luang Village in the Pua District of Nan Province is becoming a tonal language due to contact with Tai Yuan, the majority language of Nan Province. There are two groups of lexical pitches in the Ta Luang variety: high and low.
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 lexical pitch classes (high, low) in Ta Luang Mal

tone_statements.citation: Theraphan L-Thongkum and Chommanad Intajamornrak. 2008 [issued 2009]. Tonal evolution induced by language contact: A case study of the T'in (Lua') language of Nan province, northern Thailand. Mon-Khmer Studies 38 (Special volume dedicated to Dr. David Thomas): 57-68.
tone_statements.quote: Based on the Mal data collected by the first author at Yot Doi Watthana Village in Bo Kluea Tai Sub-district, we must conclude that this Mal variety has two distinctive pitches or two tones, i.e. /FALLING/ vs. /RISING/ or /HIGH/ vs. /LOW/. An acoustic study was done to confirm our analysis of the Mal tones. ... Although the falling tone in the other Mal varieties has a few variants, due to syllable-structure types, there is always a two-way tonal distinction, i.e. /Falling/ vs. /Rising/ or /High/ vs. /Low/.
tone_statements.locator: p.63, section 4 'Contact-induced tonal evolution'.. p.65, end of section 4
tone_statements.summary: Bo Kluea Mal has acquired two contrastive tones, falling [high-falling] vs rising [low-rising], also labelled high/low; F0 of 20 minimal pairs; rising mostly on Tai loans; Pray lacks consistent pitch.

sources.note: p.241 fn.1: major syllable = one that may carry primary stress, minor syllables never stressed; p.251: minor syllables 'occur only with weak stress'; Word structure = one major syllable with 0-2 PRECEDING minor syllables, hence every word has a single stress on its (final) major syllable, e.g. [pa'thia?] 'evening', [taba'pan]; p.252: in compounds the first member becomes a short-vowel minor syllable [nthu'?uago]; stressless minor syllables are lower pitched; also a system of three sentence stresses.
